design_detail: Two-site (Baylor College of Medicine, Houston; Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York), parallel-arm, double-blind randomized trial with an active placebo, November 2010 to August 2012. 73 medication-free adults with treatment-resistant major depression (inadequate response to at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials) were randomized 2:1 to one 40-minute intravenous infusion of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg or of midazolam 0.045 mg/kg, a short-acting benzodiazepine anaesthetic chosen to mimic ketamine's nonspecific sedation and disorientation; 72 were analysed (modified intention to treat: 47 ketamine, 25 midazolam). Inpatient on the infusion day with cardiovascular monitoring, discharged at 24 hours, then seen at 48 hours, 72 hours and 7 days; day-7 responders followed every 2 weeks until relapse or for 4 more weeks. Primary outcome: MADRS at 24 hours, adjusted for baseline score and site. No trial registration is reported in the version read.
can_establish: Whether, in medication-free adults with highly treatment-resistant major depression, one 40-minute infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg lowered clinician-rated depression (MADRS) 24 hours later more than an infusion of midazolam chosen to mimic nonspecific anaesthetic effects, and which adverse effects, dissociative symptoms and blood-pressure changes followed the infusion over 7 days.
cannot_establish: Whether the benefit lasts beyond a few days (no significant group difference on MADRS or response at day 7), the effect of repeated infusions or of ketamine added to ongoing antidepressants (all medication was stopped), effects in people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder or alcohol or substance abuse in the past 2 years (excluded), whether blinding held (not assessed), or rare and longer-term harms (47 people given one infusion and followed for at most about 5 weeks).

sample.recruitment: Two academic research sites; 116 patients completed informed consent and 73 met all eligibility criteria and were randomized. How patients were recruited (referral, advertisement) is not described in the main text (Method › Study Design and Patients, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21 to 80; primary major depressive disorder by SCID-P; inadequate response to at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials on the Antidepressant Treatment History Form, completed by a study psychiatrist from the patient, family or carer, pharmacy and medical records; a previous episode before the current one, or a chronic current episode of at least 2 years, with an IDS-C30 score of 32 or more at screening and within 24 hours of the infusion (the sentence's grouping is ambiguous). Excluded: lifetime psychotic illness or bipolar disorder, alcohol or substance abuse in the previous 2 years, unstable medical illness, serious and imminent suicidal or homicidal risk, MMSE below 27, contraindicated medications. Physical examination, blood tests, urine toxicology and ECG at screening (Method › Study Design and Patients, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Ketamine (47) against midazolam (25): women 26 (55%) and 11 (44%); white 37 (79%) and 23 (92%); Hispanic 7 (15%) and 3 (12%); mean age 46.9 (SD 12.8) and 42.7 (11.6); education 16.5 (2.3) and 16.2 (2.3) years; previous antidepressant failures 5.1 (2.0) and 5.0 (1.8); index episode 146.6 (158.3) and 109.2 (139.0) months, chronic (2 years or more) in 33 (70%) and 16 (64%); prior suicide attempt 14 (30%) and 9 (36%); prior psychiatric hospitalization 23 (49%) and 13 (52%); unemployed 27 (57%) and 15 (60%); body mass index 29.4 (7.5) and 27.0 (6.1); baseline MADRS 32.6 (6.1) and 31.1 (5.6), QIDS-SR16 16.6 (4.1) and 16.3 (4.5), IDS-C30 48 (9) and 48 (10) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: One patient randomized to ketamine received no study medication; the other 72 received it and completed the 24-hour assessment; 67 completed all assessments to day 7. By protocol, non-responders (less than 50% MADRS improvement) were not followed after day 7; day-7 responders who chose to continue (21 ketamine, 4 midazolam) were followed for relapse (Results › Study Participants, 1st paragraph; Method › Study Procedures, 3rd paragraph; Results › Durability of drug effect, 4th paragraph). The flow diagram is in the online supplement (Figure SF1, not read).
sample.selection_effects: Highly chronic (mean index episode 9 to 12 years) and resistant (about 5 failed trials) patients at academic research units, mostly white and with about 16 years of education, who could stop all psychotropic medication: 17.2% of screened patients refused or could not tolerate the washout (Discussion, 6th paragraph). People with any psychotic history or alcohol or substance abuse in the past 2 years were excluded. The results describe ketamine given alone, not added to an antidepressant.

exposure.measurement: Assigned infusion prepared from sealed envelopes held by the research pharmacist, given over 40 minutes after an overnight fast through an antecubital catheter, with pulse, blood pressure, pulse oximetry and ECG monitoring in a clinical research unit (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). No blood levels were measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one intravenous infusion over 40 minutes of ketamine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/kg or midazolam 0.045 mg/kg; the authors describe the midazolam dose as equipotent to the ketamine dose and chose midazolam for its fast onset and short elimination half-life (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol or substance abuse in the previous 2 years excluded and urine toxicology done at screening; patients were told to abstain from substances and alcohol at home after discharge, without reported verification. Tobacco use not reported (Method › Study Design and Patients, 1st paragraph; Study Procedures, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Free of antidepressants and other psychotropic medication for at least 1 week before the infusion (at least 4 weeks for fluoxetine) and throughout, except a stable dose of a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic; how this was verified is not stated (Method › Study Procedures, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: An infusion of midazolam as an active placebo: an anaesthetic benzodiazepine intended to mimic the time course of ketamine's nonspecific effects (sedation, disorientation) without specific antidepressant effects, given on the same schedule and with the same monitoring (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 2:1; the research pharmacist prepared sealed envelopes containing the drug identity, and investigators, anaesthesiologists, raters, patients and data analysts were masked. How the sequence was generated is not described (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph). The groups are described as well matched (Table 1), with some differences: women 55% against 44%, index episode 147 against 109 months, atypical features 9% against 24%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population and the same medication-free condition.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: clinician-administered MADRS (0 to 60) 24 hours after the infusion. Secondary: MADRS response (a fall of 50% or more from baseline); QIDS-SR16 (self-rated, 0 to 27); Clinical Global Impression severity and improvement; durability of benefit up to day 7 (MADRS and response at 1, 2, 3 and 7 days); time to relapse in day-7 responders (relapse: MADRS of 20 or more at two consecutive visits and meeting criteria for a major depressive episode for 1 week). Safety: a modified Patient Rated Inventory of Side Effects (general adverse events; sleep and sexual domains excluded) at 40, 120 and 240 minutes and 24 hours, 48 hours, 72 hours and 7 days; Clinician-Administered Dissociative States Scale (dissociation) and BPRS positive symptom subscale (psychotic-type symptoms) at regular intervals; blood pressure at baseline, 40 and 240 minutes (Method › Outcomes; Table 3 footnotes; Table 4; Figure 3 legend). Symptom ratings were made during the infusion and to 240 minutes after its start; the primary outcome at 24 hours was chosen to fall after the acute psychoactive effects (Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Method › Outcomes, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-outcome raters were experienced, trained research staff, with MADRS conventions pilot-tested in earlier ketamine studies; interrater reliability between the two primary raters at each site 0.988 (Method › Outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit = lower MADRS at 24 hours after ketamine than after midazolam in a general linear model adjusted for baseline MADRS and site, with Cohen's d; response by exact logistic regression adjusted for site; durability by mixed models of days 1 to 7 with treatment, time and their interaction. Dissociative symptoms are reported as significant in 8 patients without a stated threshold in the main text (Method › Statistical Analysis; Results › Adverse Events, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; every test used P ≤ 0.05 (Method › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph). Six efficacy outcomes (MADRS, response, QIDS-SR16, CGI severity, CGI improvement, relapse), several of them at 24 hours, over days 1 to 7 and at day 7.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Investigators, anaesthesiologists, raters, patients and data analysts were masked; primary-outcome raters were not involved in infusion-day procedures and were unaware of infusion-related side effects (Method › Study Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Outcomes, 1st paragraph). No check of what patients or raters guessed is reported; the Discussion notes that dissociative effects right after the infusion were more frequent with ketamine (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: MADRS at 24 hours lower after ketamine by 7.95 points (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71) after adjustment for baseline and site, Cohen's d 0.81; means 14.77 (95% CI 11.73 to 17.80) and 22.72 (18.85 to 26.59), t = 3.34, df = 68. Response at 24 hours 30 of 47 (64%) against 7 of 25 (28%), odds ratio 2.18 (1.21 to 4.14), P ≤ 0.006, number needed to treat 2.8. Editors' calculation from these counts: risk difference 35.8 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 54.2, Newcombe method); crude odds ratio 4.54 (1.58 to 13.05). QIDS-SR16 lower by 3.40 (0.78 to 6.01), d 0.63. CGI improvement rated much or very much improved 29 (62%) against 6 (24%), odds ratio 2.31 (1.25 to 4.66); CGI severity minimally or not ill 25 (53%) against 2 (8%), odds ratio 4.08 (1.76 to 13.51). Days 1 to 7: treatment F(1,202) = 5.93, P ≤ 0.02, time F = 7.62, treatment × time F = 0.31 (P ≤ 0.58); mean MADRS across the 4 days 16.93 (14.03 to 19.82) against 23.19 (19.03 to 27.34). Day 7: MADRS, QIDS-SR16, response and CGI improvement not significantly different; CGI severity of 2 or less, odds ratio 2.26 (1.07 to 5.76).
analysis.covariates: Baseline score and site for MADRS, QIDS-SR16 and CGI; site only for response; site in the days 1 to 7 mixed models (Method › Statistical Analysis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The version read (NIH author manuscript) names no trial registry, registration number, protocol or analysis plan. The publisher's page (psychiatryonline.org) showed a check page and was not read, so whether the published version reports a registration is not known.
analysis.selective_reporting: The day-7 results (Table ST1), dissociative and psychotic-symptom scores (Table ST2, Figure SF2), serious adverse events (Table ST3) and the flow diagram (Figure SF1) are only in the online data supplement, a PDF that was not read; the day-7 null results and the statement that ketamine did not increase psychotic or manic symptoms depend on it. The durability and relapse results are shown mainly as Figures 1 to 3, images whose values were not extracted. The midazolam group's rate of dissociative symptoms is not given in the main text. Sensitivity analyses for missing data are mentioned but not reported.
analysis.power: 72 patients (2:1) gave 80% power for a MADRS difference of Cohen's d 0.71 and 96% for response rates of 60% against 15% at 24 hours, two-tailed α 0.05 (Method › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph); 72 were analysed and the observed d was 0.81.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Twenty-four hours after one infusion, MADRS was about 8 points lower after ketamine than after midazolam (7.95, 95% CI 3.20 to 12.71) and 64% against 28% met response criteria (editors' risk difference 36 percentage points, 12 to 54); the self-rated QIDS-SR16 and both CGI measures agreed. Over days 1 to 7 the ketamine group stayed lower on average, but at day 7 the groups no longer differed significantly on MADRS, QIDS-SR16, response or CGI improvement. After ketamine, 17% had dissociative symptoms that resolved within 2 hours, blurred vision, dizziness and nausea were more common than after midazolam, systolic pressure rose from 121.7 to 140.7 mm Hg at 40 minutes, and 2 of 47 infusions were stopped for blood-pressure or heart-rate changes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that ketamine showed rapid antidepressant effects in an optimized design and asks for more information on durability and safety, which matches the data; its odds ratio for response (2.18) is smaller than the odds ratio implied by its own percentages (editors' 4.5; see reporting issues). The Discussion goes further: “We consistently demonstrated the magnitude and duration of ketamine’s benefit” across two sites (2nd paragraph), although no group difference remained at day 7; it suggests that the infusion is safe in the short term for nonpsychotic depressed patients on the basis of 47 people, 2 of whose infusions were stopped (3rd paragraph); and the conclusion presents the active placebo as showing an effect specific to ketamine apart from its anaesthetic properties (7th paragraph), although blinding was not checked and dissociation was more frequent after ketamine. The authors acknowledge that no control condition is perfect, that only one infusion and a brief follow-up were tested, and that ketamine added to ongoing treatment was not studied (Discussion, 4th and 6th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Zarate et al.: NIMH crossover trial, 18 inpatients, the same ketamine dose against saline; HDRS lower from 110 minutes to day 7, day-1 response 12 of 17 against 0 of 14. Dennis S. Charney is an author of both trials.
This trial: 72 analysed at two sites against midazolam; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours, response 64% against 28%, no significant difference at day 7.

Daly et al.: esketamine nasal spray added to oral antidepressants, 67 randomized; in period 1, MADRS 9.1 to 10.7 points lower than placebo at 24 hours and 5.0 to 10.5 points lower at day 8 (a different drug form, route and design).

replication.where_it_stands: The 24-hour effect is consistent with the earlier saline-controlled crossover trial (Zarate et al., 2006), which shares one author with this trial, and with the 24-hour results of a later trial of esketamine nasal spray (Daly et al., 2018), which used a different drug form, route and design. The two trials of intravenous ketamine disagree on day 7 (significant against saline, not against midazolam). No later trial of intravenous ketamine against midazolam was read in this round; the systematic reviews on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023) are being read by other readers.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, multi-site trial against an active placebo in which patients and raters record which treatment they think was given, every participant (not only responders) is followed for at least 4 weeks with repeated or single infusions as randomized, ketamine is also tested alongside usual antidepressant treatment, and absolute response and relapse rates are reported per arm at fixed times.

domains.note: Randomized 2:1 with sealed envelopes prepared by the research pharmacist and everyone else masked, but how the sequence was generated is not described. Baseline characteristics are broadly balanced, with modest differences in sex (55% against 44% women), index-episode length and atypical features.

A single masked infusion; one patient randomized to ketamine was not treated and is excluded from the modified intention-to-treat set (1 of 73). Two ketamine infusions stopped early for haemodynamic changes are not described as excluded.

Primary outcome available for 72 of 73 randomized. Later outcomes are less complete (67 at day 7) and relapse was followed in responders only, by design, so relapse data describe only those who responded.

The primary-outcome raters were kept apart from infusion-day procedures and side effects, and midazolam gives some sedation; but patients, whose answers make up the MADRS interview and the QIDS-SR16, could recognise ketamine's dissociative effects (17% had significant dissociative symptoms), and no check of blinding is reported.
The primary outcome and its 24-hour time point are justified in the article, and the analyses are described, but no registration, protocol or analysis plan is cited in the version read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This trial addresses the main weakness of the earlier saline-controlled studies with an active placebo, raters shielded from infusion-day effects, two sites and almost complete 24-hour data. The remaining concerns are that blinding was not checked for a drug whose acute effects patients notice, that the version read reports no registration, and that sequence generation is not described. The source can be cited for a 24-hour difference of about 8 MADRS points and response in 64% against 28% after one infusion in medication-free adults with highly treatment-resistant depression, and for the transient dissociation, adverse effects and blood-pressure rise that followed; it cannot be cited for benefit lasting a week or more, for ketamine added to other treatment, or for safety beyond the first week.

key_findings.finding: 116 patients consented; 73 were randomized 2:1; one patient randomized to ketamine did not receive study medication; 72 received it and completed the 24-hour assessments (47 ketamine, 25 midazolam); 67 completed all assessments to day 7.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1 column headings

key_findings.finding: Baseline (ketamine against midazolam): women 55% and 44%; mean age 46.9 and 42.7; previous antidepressant failures 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 5.0 (1.8); index episode 146.6 and 109.2 months; prior suicide attempt 30% and 36%; MADRS 32.6 (6.1) and 31.1 (5.6); QIDS-SR16 16.6 (4.1) and 16.3 (4.5).

Primary outcome: 24 hours after the infusion, MADRS was lower in the ketamine group by 7.95 points (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71) after adjustment for baseline score and site, Cohen's d 0.81; mean MADRS 14.77 (95% CI 11.73 to 17.80) against 22.72 (18.85 to 26.59), t = 3.34, df = 68; 24-hour scores did not differ by site (F = 0.63, df = 1, 70, P = 0.43).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome; Table 2, MADRS row and footnote b

key_findings.finding: Response (a MADRS fall of 50% or more) at 24 hours: 30 of 47 (64%) after ketamine against 7 of 25 (28%) after midazolam; odds ratio 2.18 (95% CI 1.21 to 4.14), P ≤ 0.006; number needed to treat 2.8; responder status did not differ by site (exact P = 0.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Additional 24-hour outcomes; Table 2, Response row
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: risk difference 35.8 percentage points (95% CI 11.6 to 54.2, Newcombe method); crude odds ratio 4.54 (1.58 to 13.05). The printed odds ratio is about the square root of the crude one (see reporting issues); cite the counts and percentages.

key_findings.finding: Other 24-hour outcomes: QIDS-SR16 mean 8.38 (95% CI 6.71 to 10.05) against 11.78 (9.63 to 13.92), adjusted difference 3.40 (0.78 to 6.01), P ≤ 0.02, d 0.63; CGI improvement much or very much improved 29 (62%) against 6 (24%), odds ratio 2.31 (1.25 to 4.66); CGI severity minimally or not at all ill 25 (53%) against 2 (8%), odds ratio 4.08 (1.76 to 13.51).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Additional 24-hour outcomes; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Days 1, 2, 3 and 7 (mixed model adjusted for site): main effects of time (F = 7.62, df = 1, 202, P ≤ 0.006) and treatment (F = 5.93, df = 1, 202, P ≤ 0.02) but no treatment × time interaction (F = 0.31, P ≤ 0.58); both groups worsened slightly with each day; averaged over the 4 days, MADRS 16.93 (95% CI 14.03 to 19.82) after ketamine against 23.19 (19.03 to 27.34) after midazolam (t = 2.44, df = 202, P ≤ 0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 1st paragraph; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Response over days 1 to 7: main effects of time (F = 8.04, P ≤ 0.006) and treatment (F = 6.61, P ≤ 0.02), no treatment × time interaction (F = 0.12, P ≤ 0.73).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Day 7, adjusted for site and baseline: MADRS and QIDS-SR16 no longer differed significantly between groups, nor did the response rate or the proportion much or very much improved on the CGI; CGI severity of 2 or less was more likely after ketamine (odds ratio 2.26, 95% CI 1.07 to 5.76).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The day-7 estimates are in supplement Table ST1, which was not read.

key_findings.finding: At day 7, 4 patients in the midazolam group and 21 in the ketamine group still met response criteria and chose to continue; their time to relapse over the next 4 weeks is shown only in Figure 3 (relapse: MADRS of 20 or more at two consecutive visits and a major depressive episode for 1 week).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 4th paragraph; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: Figure 3 is an image; no relapse times or rates were extracted.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events on the infusion day (new or worse, ketamine against midazolam): dizziness 21 (45%) and 5 (20%); blurred vision 20 (43%) and 2 (8%); nausea or vomiting 16 (34%) and 3 (12%); headache 15 (32%) and 5 (20%); dry mouth 12 (26%) and 4 (16%); poor coordination 12 (26%) and 3 (12%); poor concentration 12 (26%) and 2 (8%), rated distressing by 9 (19%) and 0; tremors 6 (13%) and 0; anxiety 7 (15%) and 0; restlessness 10 (21%) and 5 (20%); general malaise 3 (6%) and 7 (28%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Infusion Day columns; Results › Adverse Events, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Modified Patient Rated Inventory of Side Effects at 40, 120 and 240 minutes after the infusion (Table 3 footnotes).

key_findings.finding: Adverse events on days 1 to 7 (new or worse, ketamine against midazolam): restlessness 19 (printed 41%) and 7 (28%); anxiety 14 (30%) and 7 (28%); headache 15 (32%) and 7 (28%); poor concentration 12 (26%) and 3 (12%); dry skin 12 (26%) and 5 (20%); frequent urination 4 (9%) and 0; painful urination 3 (6%) and 0; difficulty urinating 1 (2%) and 0.
key_findings.note: Measured at 24, 48 and 72 hours and 7 days. Editors' calculation: 19 of 47 is 40.4%.

key_findings.finding: Eight of 47 patients given ketamine (17%) had significant dissociative symptoms (feeling outside the body, time passing more slowly or quickly) immediately after the infusion, resolved by 2 hours; no severe psychotic symptoms (paranoia, hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder) occurred in any patient.
key_findings.note: The threshold for significant dissociation is not stated in the main text; the CADSS and BPRS data are in supplement Table ST2 and Figure SF2, not read.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure (mean, SD): ketamine systolic 121.7 (13.8) at baseline, 140.7 (17.8) at 40 minutes and 125.4 (17.6) at 240 minutes, diastolic 71.7 (11.3), 80.8 (12.7) and 70.6 (8.9); midazolam systolic 120.8 (17.5), 111.8 (14.8) and 113.9 (13.0), diastolic 72.4 (9.6), 67.9 (9.9) and 71.6 (7.7). Two ketamine infusions were stopped: one after 30 minutes for a rise to 187/91 mm Hg not responding to a beta-blocker (normal within 10 minutes of stopping), and one for transient, pronounced hypotension and bradycardia that resolved, followed by overnight hospital observation.

Power: 72 patients randomized 2:1 gave 80% power for a MADRS difference of d 0.71 and 96% for response rates of 60% against 15% at 24 hours (two-tailed α 0.05); analysis by modified intention to treat (randomized, baseline and at least one later measurement).
17.2% of screened patients refused or could not tolerate the psychotropic medication washout before randomization.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed odds ratio for response (2.18, 95% CI 1.21 to 4.14) does not match the counts: 30 of 47 against 7 of 25 give a crude odds ratio of 4.54 (Woolf 95% CI 1.58 to 13.05), whose square root (2.13, 1.26 to 3.61) is close to the printed value; the same holds for CGI improvement (printed 2.31; crude 5.10, square root 2.26) (editors' calculation). This is what happens when treatment is coded −1 and +1 in a logistic model, which halves the log odds ratio; the Fisher exact P from the counts (0.006) matches the printed P ≤ 0.006.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Secondary Outcomes › Additional 24-hour outcomes; Table 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: The odds ratios understate the two-group odds ratio by about half on the log scale; claims should use the counts, the percentages (64% against 28%) and the risk difference (36 percentage points).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 footnote c gives the QIDS-SR16 test as t = 6.69, df = 68, P ≤ 0.01, while the text gives an adjusted difference of 3.40 (95% CI 0.78 to 6.01), P ≤ 0.02. The interval implies t of about 2.59 and P of about 0.012, and 2.59 squared is 6.7 (editors' calculation), so the printed statistic is probably an F value labelled t. Footnote b gives P ≤ 0.001 for the primary MADRS test (t = 3.34, df = 68), which corresponds to P = 0.0014; the Figure 1 legend gives P ≤ 0.002.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 2 footnotes b and c; Results › Secondary Outcomes › Additional 24-hour outcomes; Figure 1 legend)
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling and rounding errors; the text's P ≤ 0.02 for the QIDS-SR16 and the legend's P ≤ 0.002 for the MADRS are the values consistent with the intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the response rate no longer differed significantly at day 7, yet 21 patients given ketamine and 4 given midazolam still met response criteria at day 7 and chose to continue. If these were all day-7 responders (45% of 47 against 16% of 25), Fisher's exact test would give P = 0.02 (editors' calculation); the day-7 response figures are only in supplement Table ST1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 3rd and 4th paragraphs)
reporting_issues.consequence: The day-7 response result cannot be reconciled from the main text; claims about day 7 should rest on the stated non-significance with this caveat, or on the supplement once read.

reporting_issues.issue: The days 1 to 7 model reports a worsening of b = 0.0004 (95% CI 0.00009 to 0.00062) for each additional day after the infusion, a change far too small to be in MADRS points per day; the unit of time (or of the outcome) in the model is not stated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Secondary Outcomes › Durability of drug effect, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The slope cannot be interpreted; only the direction (slight worsening in both groups) can be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 percentages: restlessness on days 1 to 7 after ketamine, 19 of 47, printed 41% (40.4%); distressing blurred vision on days 1 to 7, 1 of 47, printed 1% (2.1%); distressing ringing in the ears on days 1 to 7, 2 of 47, printed 2% (4.3%); one midazolam cell printed as 0) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial rounding and typesetting errors; use the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The version read is the NIH author manuscript. Its footnotes say that the other authors report no financial relationships with commercial interests, but the preceding disclosures that sentence refers to are missing, and the manuscript names no trial registration.
reporting_issues.consequence: Conflicts of interest and registration status cannot be stated from this reading; the published version (psychiatryonline.org, blocked by a check page in this session) should be checked.
